en: Having worshipped all the deities dwelling upon the ground of the caitya and other sites— the world-protectors, nāgas, the Earth-goddess, and the Bodhisattvas— the knower of the ritual should perform this with the external rite and with the mind.
He stands in the center of the middle portion, purified by the circle of the earth's regions.

All those deities who dwell upon the foundation of the earth, such as stūpas and the like, as well as the guardians of the directions, nāgas, the kings of the earth, and the bodhisattvas—these external assemblies should be honored with offerings by one who knows the mental phenomena, while abiding in the center of the utterly pure essence of a portion of the earth.
With eyes [perceiving] the spheres of earth, water, fire, and wind,
he beheld the universal vajra atop the summit of Mount Meru;
by means of the massed nets of its rays, a net of arrows and vajras—
Its interior was well protected by walls, lattices, and canopies.

From the entire mandalas of earth, water, fire, and wind, Mount Meru arises perfectly; at its summit is a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*). With the masses of its lattice of light rays, one should thoroughly protect [the site] with lattices of arrows, vajra fences, pavilions, and canopies.

Having meditated with a focused mind upon a celestial palace in the sky amidst the assembly of Śrī Siṃhavikrama Samādhi Gaṇa, consisting of the *bhrūṃ* syllable, the wheel, and the rays of light of the Jina, and containing a perfectly complete Saṅgha;
To monasteries, palaces, thickets, pavilions, and temples.

Through the glorious *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*, one should mentally visualize the celestial palace arising from the syllable *bhūṃ* and the light rays of the Victorious One’s wheel in the midst of space; it is completely filled with monasteries, palatial mansions, houses, guesthouses, and temples, all thoroughly occupied by the Saṅgha.
One should worship all those situated in the center of the lotus— the bricks and so forth, which consist of a collection of atoms of light rays from the syllable *Bhrūṃ*—
possessing beautiful, fully developed, perfectly ripe, and supremely radiant peaks.
Or with sandalwood and saffron sprinkled with fragrant water.

The light from the syllable *Bhrūṃ* transforms the entire collection of atoms, including the hogs and so forth, into those who abide in the center of lotuses; these should be perfectly worshipped. They are complete, beautiful with the supreme radiance of the Dharma, and possess elegant proportions; they should be anointed with fragrant water, red sandalwood, and saffron.
All these [trees] have their tops and horns broken and infested by anthills, insects, and woodworms, and are marked with the footprints of wild beasts;
shaking them off, [one should worship] with *phalinī* flowers, with blossoms white as vermilion powder and fragrant *tila* paste.
% Huh?

% It was eaten by swarms of ants and termites; it was broken, its corners damaged, and entirely covered with the hoofprints of cattle and turned yellowish-brown. Having discarded these and removed them, [he offered] *ku* flowers, blossoms, *lebrgan* resin, *sindūra*, white *akhurba*, the *brahman’s thread* (*brahmasūtra*), sesame seeds, and so forth.
And having gratified the assembly of master craftsmen and artisans, who were possessed of great skill,
with golden bracelets,
beautiful rings for the hands and fingers, garments, gold, food, drink, and guvāka flowers;
Having thoroughly satisfied the spectators and the lord of men.

They shall be thoroughly satisfied; the skilled masons and the assembly of artisans shall be fully gratified with golden bracelets, earrings, finger-rings, garments, gold, food, drink, ornaments, and flowers. Both the spectators and the lord of men shall likewise be completely satisfied.
Having beheld the moon and sun of the Tathāgatas facing east and north, the preceptor and chief artisan, his heart full of nourishment,
[performed the rite] bound by the life-force situated on the earth along the paths of the moon and sun.
One should place [it] upon a vessel made of silver or gold.

Facing north and east, having gazed upon the Tathāgatas and the moon and sun, with an expansive mind, the Guru and the chief artisan, while the earth-winds move along the paths of the moon and sun, shall begin the work and place the silver and gold skeletal frames upon the foundation.

Placed with their northern ends facing Indra (the east), with steady minds, in the sequence beginning from the pitcher at the southeast corner (āgneyakoṇa) and proceeding according to the Nandyāvarta pattern,
there shall be a mandala of bricks extending for a thousand [units] in every direction.
% Huh?

% By means of the mind first made firm through abiding in the east and the north, if one joins them in due order by circling to the right toward the southeast and other directions, it will be perfected; for the bricks are laid out within the thousandfold perimeter of the quarters.
Having rung the bell with a joyful mind and placing it there with the right hand, one should first recite mantras while facing the intermediate directions; then,
the consecration with the water from the vases of Vairocana and the other [deities] should be performed.
Having accepted [the disciple] with the ritual of the five offerings by means of the disciples.

Suvajrapāṇi should ring the bell and, with the vajra firmly held in his right hand, perform the recitation; then, having first sprinkled the directions with water from the vases of Vairocana and the others, the disciple should receive the ritual of the five services (pañcopacāra).
At that time, when the assembly of joyful people was filled with a flood of bliss through the recitations of the true Dharma by the hosts of sons of the Sugata,
and when those who were naked, emaciated, wretched, and destitute were set free;
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable zodiacal sign and other such conditions, amidst the sounds of abundant musical performances.

When the assembly of the Sugata’s sons has filled [the place] and the sublime Dharma is being recited; when people gather with great joy and there is a time of universal delight; and when those who are naked and physically debilitated are thoroughly liberated from suffering—at that juncture of virtuous qualities and the right moment, one should first perform music, song, and melody.
Having placed bricks and other materials there, the donor, encouraged by merit and the like,
should cause a downpour of water from the clouds to fall in all directions.

One should cause the stream of the water of virtue to flow and spread in all directions by means of those who have established clay seals and the like, through the sincere encouragement of donors, scholars, and others.
A great and most auspicious [pavilion] should be half a man's height wider than its length;
its level terrace should be one-third of that width, and it should have a peak like a rutting elephant.
% Huh? A broken *gīti*?

% Regarding the temple (*gtsug lag khang*), it is best when its length exceeds half [the standard] and its width is large. The raised platform (*stegs bu*) and the peak for protecting against intoxication (*myos pa bsrung ba'i rtse mo*) should be equal to three-quarters of the width.

In that same manner, one should construct the *gartāpūra* (filling of the pit), the *mekhalikā* (girdle), and the fire-preventing masonry; or alternatively, one may extend it as far as the water-stone (*vāriśilā*). Having carefully considered the wall, the measurement for the ground situated at the *ehalikā* (the base of the plinth) should be such that each individual section—such as the *kaṇṭhikā* (neck) and so forth—is one-third of the length from the pinnacle.

The filling of the hollows is likewise taught to be done with cords, fire, arrows, or even water and stones; as for the walls, they should be constructed by consultation. Regarding the uncarved [wood], the measurement extends to the end of the beam; likewise, the length extending to the tip of the pinnacle shall be three parts, and each part is a *mahā-aṃśa*.

The lattice-work between the pillars is prescribed as fifty parts. The wooden beams, measured by their length, consist of portions that are either broken or complete and arranged in a series of circles. On the fifth part of the altar (vedī), at a distance of two parts, the great wall has a width of two parts. Measuring five parts of that [wall], the bricks are two parts long; among those measuring five parts in length, bricks with a width of three parts are recommended. Therein, the entire division of the temple (prāsāda) is one part in height.

The pillars and the inner lattice are said to be three-fifths [of the total]. In the circular garland that completes the parts and their subdivisions, the wooden rafters are equal in measure. On the pedestal, two-fifths of the five parts constitute the width of the great wall. Of that wall, two-fifths of the five parts is the measurement for the length of the cornice. Its length is also five parts.
The field is taught to possess three parts; one-third of those three parts is the height, which constitutes all the portions of the palace.
Oṃ bhrūṃ! May all the Tathāgatas, all the Buddhas, consecrate this brick; svāhā! Thus, one should consecrate the brick seven times at each corner.
*oṃ bhrūṃ sarvatathāgata-sarvabuddhāvalaye ādhitiṣṭhantu svāhā*. With this, one should consecrate each of the individual corners seven times.

Then, having gratified the guardians of the directions and others with a peace-offering homa, one should perform a rite for the peace of the king and the lord of the gifts, and offer the remaining oblation.

Then, having fully propitiated the guardians of the directions and others through the peaceful fire offering (*śānti-homa*), one should also pacify the lord of the earth and the lord of the donors, and offer the remaining *bali* oblation.
In the subsequent ritual procedures, a festival should be celebrated according to one's capacity; furthermore, one should provide a communal feast and offer a sacrificial fee to the Guru.
As before and here as well, one should perform the rituals according to one's capacity with enthusiasm, and offer a feast for the Saṅgha and a gift of honor to the Guru.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of honor (*argha*) to monasteries, shrines, perfumed chambers, the Saṅgha, hermitages, and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual for making offerings to monasteries, stupas, perfume chambers, and residential dwellings.

In the construction of lotus ponds, large tanks, wells, and so forth, one should first perform offerings and worship, and having prepared the *argha* water and other requisites, one should meditate on Vairocana in the form of Vajravaruṇa by reciting "Oṃ Vaṃ Vajravaruṇa Hūṃ. Then, having recited "Oṃ Vajrasattva Samayas Tvaṃ," one should cast a flower and visualize [the site] as filled with the water of the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), the abode of the eight families of *nāgas*, extending down to the subterranean realm (*ārasātala*). This is the ritual procedure for the *argha* offering for lotus ponds and the like.

When constructing ponds, springs, wells, and so forth, one should first perform the *bali* offering and worship. Having presented the water for offerings (*argha*) and other requisites, one should visualize oneself as Vairocana through the mantra *oṃ vaṃ vajrabaruṇa hūṃ*, transforming into the form of Vajra Varuṇa. From that transformation, one arises and fills the site—the abode of the eight classes of *nāgas*—with the water of the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānāmṛta*). Then, *oṃ vajra...* [and so on].

Reciting "satva samayas tvam," one should scatter flowers and visualize that [the ground] is filled with water possessing the eight qualities, reaching down to the great foundation. This is the ritual for the arghya offering at ponds and so forth.

In the making of images—whether by casting, carving, painting, or molding—the artisan, preceded by worship and offerings, should instantly visualize the forms of the family lords (*kulādhipa*) of the deity to be fashioned. These are to be visualized as being joined with their respective seed-syllables (*svabīja*) at the heart, throat, and crown in due order, along with the syllables *HŪṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ* situated upon a vajra, lotus, and wheel, and further joined by a moon and a vajra in the left and right hands respectively. Then, touching their hearts and other parts with his right hand holding a vajra, he consecrates them with the syllables *BHŪḤ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ*.

Having visualized the materials—wood, clay, stone, or cloth—which have been purified by the procedure to be described, as being within emptiness and instantly possessing the form of the deity to be fashioned by means of the seed-syllable in the heart, one should recite the passage beginning with "O Blessed One" and ending with "you should grant your presence," as will be stated below. In all such cases here, the dismissal of the visualized deities must be performed; this is the ritual for the *argha* offering for images and the like.

When fashioning images—whether cast, carved, or painted—one should first perform offerings and *bali* rituals. Then, having fashioned the artisan into the form of the presiding deity of the respective family, one should place the syllables *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ* upon the heart, throat, and head respectively, abiding on a vajra, a lotus, and a wheel.

One should visualize in a single instant the syllables *daṃ*, *aṃ*, and *oṃ* upon the left and right hands as being endowed with a moon disc and a vajra; then, touching the heart and other parts with the right hand together with the vajra while reciting *hūṃ āḥ oṃ*, one should consecrate them.

By means of the purificatory ritual that brings about transformation, one should mentally visualize, in an instant, pure substances such as wood, clay, or stone as being empty, and subsequently as the form of a deity produced by the seed-syllable at the heart; [this continues] from "O Bhagavān... up to "...the lineage of those who provide presence."

The ultimate [conclusions] of these points will be explained later; they shall now be stated. In all cases here, one should request the deities who have been meditated upon to depart. This concludes the ritual for the offering water (arghya) for the images and so forth.

[After one and a half lines of deletion marks] However, in the case of writing the *saddharma*, preceded by worship and offerings, one should visualize the syllable *dhīḥ* upon a leaf consisting of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*). Then, having visualized the scribe—purified as before in the form of Amitābha—as being transformed into the form of letters through mutual passion, [the scribe] being composed of the *vajradharma* nature of the Perfectly Awakened Ones summoned by its rays and consisting of the echoes of the nine-limbed *saddharma*. And oneself, with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ*.

Having empowered the pen with "Oṃ Āḥ Vighnāntakṛt Hūṃ" and the ink-pot twenty-one times, one should place the ink-pot, shaped like a *dharmodayā*, in the left hand of the scribe and the pen, in the form of a *vajra*, in the right. Then, having cast [the ink] with the mantra: "Oṃ Dhīḥ! O you who are victorious through hearing and memory, O remover of the veil of all ignorance, Hrīḥ Svāhā!"—one should contemplate that as the union of the ink-pot and the pen occurs, the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) flashes forth, and whatever is to be written is thereby accomplished. One should also dismiss the visualized deity.

In the *Śrutismṛtivijaya*, when inquiring into the sublime Dharma, one should first perform offerings and *bali* rituals. Then, having visualized the pages—which are the nature of the five wisdoms—as the syllable *dhīḥ*, the Perfect Buddhas invited by its light rays appear in the form of Vajradharma.

The nine-limbed sublime dharmas are the mutual resonance of their respective sounds; they are the complete transformation of the syllable *āḥ*, which does not deviate from its preceding state. The scribes, having first purified themselves, should visualize themselves in the form of Amitābha. One should also [visualize] the brush with *oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ* and the ink with *oṃ āḥ*.

With the mantra *bighnāntakṛte hūṃ*, consecrate the ink vessel twenty-one times. Then, place the ink vessel, which is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), in the left hand of the scribe, and give him the stylus, which is of the nature of a vajra, in his right hand. Recite: *oṃ dhīḥ śruti smṛti vijaye sarvajñānapratilambhāpāriṇi hrīḥ svāhā*.

Having established [the mandala] with this mantra, one should prepare ink and a pen; then, whatever is written with the radiance of wisdom and primordial gnosis (jñāna), one should contemplate that it is completely perfected. One should also request the visualized deities to depart. Thus it is said.
One should abandon for the sake of the true Dharma a waist-cloth, a sacred thread, ink, a thief, a cowrie shell, a crooked person, and a person with a distorted disposition.
What is a wrong livelihood?
One who possesses a staff, a water-pot, and a sacred thread; one with a blackened body and matted locks.
Those who live wickedly and are full of deceit completely abandon the purpose of the sublime Dharma.
At the beginning, the first page should be written with the bottom edge [of the leaf];
afterwards, it should be written with the top edge by a scribe who desires the welfare [of the work].
Having begun with the first petal, one should draw it well according to the proportions of the base.
Later, it was correctly inscribed by Rtse-mo; the scribe belonged to the Phan-pa lineage.
One should perform its application according to the sequence of the back of the head (kolapṛṣṭha).
Having divided it into five equal parts, one should discard three parts with the right hand.
Just as with the sequence on the back of the *kula*, so too should that garland be formed.
Having made five parts equal, discard three parts on the right.
"Leaving two parts on the left, a piercing in the middle brings auspiciousness"— this is the definition of the single-pierced [needle].
"Leaving two parts on the left, a piercing in the middle attains virtue"— this is the characteristic of the single-pierced [needle].
Having divided it into three equal parts, one should pierce it twice for the arising of auspiciousness.
Having made the three equal, the second aperture increases virtue.
Thus concludes the noble ritual for the transcription of the True Dharma.
Thus concludes the ritual for the offering of the drinking water (*argha*) when inquiring about the sublime Dharma.
Those images of shrines and the like situated in monasteries and gabled halls, which have become exceedingly worn and decayed—
broken, scorched, shattered, or with limbs cracked— they do not lead to the welfare of the king who gave them as a gift.

Whatever temples, multi-storied mansions, or residential chambers exist, and whatever ancient stūpas, images, and the like are decayed by wood, broken, shattered, fragmented, or have their parts withered—these bring no auspiciousness to the kings who are their patrons.
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare, merit, and liberation of kings who bestow protection upon the circle of their subjects, as well as for those seeking excellence,
the preeminent master Prāvīṇa should diligently carry out the restoration of those who have fallen into decay and the like.

Therefore, for the sake of the supreme goal, merit, and liberation, kings who are the benefactors of living beings must diligently restore and accomplish those [teachings] that have become corrupted, through the efforts of the most excellent and preeminent masters.
Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, or having joined them together and informed the hosts of lords of sages,
let the guardians of the directions and all the gods bear witness.
One should [propitiate] the lords of the sites by means of fire offerings and the distribution of sacrificial oblations.

Having worshipped the assembly of the Lord of Sages with offerings such as flowers and so forth, one should make a formal supplication; then, having appointed them as witnesses, one should thoroughly offer burnt sacrifices and ritual cakes (bali) to the guardians of the directions, all the gods, and the lords of the site.
Having satisfied [the deities] and having ascertained the most excellent auspiciousness of the stars, planets, time, and moment,
he whose self is the manifestation of Śrī Vajrasattva and the others—
May my excellent preceptor perform the ritual action.

Having satisfied [the deities], one should definitively examine the constellations, planets, and seasons for their auspiciousness and purity. Then, with an identity visualized as the glorious Vajrasattva and others, the master, together with his inner circle, shall accomplish the rites.
Having recited his own mantras one hundred and eight times,
he whose hands bear the vajra-mark, who is of firm prowess and noble birth,
binds the image with five-stranded garlands.
That which follows from knowledge is the vessel situated within the heart.

Having recited one hundred and eight of his own secret mantras, the vajra-teacher, firm and heroic in his hand-symbol, binds the rosary and its five threads; then, from the heart of that wisdom-family image, he acts with speed.
Having drawn forth the seed-syllable situated upon the lotus, which has been made into a mass of eggs containing the syllable *hoḥ*,
by means of the rites such as sprinkling and the discharge of arrows.
One should establish it for the sake of non-contrariety.

Having summoned [the deities] and visualized the seed-syllables arranged in rows at their birthplaces, with the syllable *hoḥ* as the heart, one should meditate on the discordant positions according to the ritual procedure preceded by the offerings and so forth.
In a pure, beautiful, new vessel marked with signs and filled with the five nectars and other substances,
[one should contemplate] the pure body situated within the interior of the vessel.
One should worship it constantly with an unwearied mind.

The vase, beautiful and newly adorned with excellent marks, completely pure, should be filled with the five nectars and so forth. One should always perfectly worship the pure body residing within the vase, which possesses a stable nature.
This old image, made of stone or earth, should be moved by artisans using mechanical devices and the like,
and then cast into the waters of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Or rather, [is it] within the interior of mountain caves and the like?

These mechanical devices, fashioned by the hands of artisans, are images made of stone or aged earth; these should be cast into the rivers of the non-Buddhists, or otherwise into deep mountain caves and the like.
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer as an oblation something made of wood, bound with new cloth and smeared with oil and clarified butter;
or, having reduced a material substance to a liquid state, one should offer it.
One should pour the most perfect [nectar] into that which consists of truth.

If it is of the nature of wood, one should bind it with new cloth, anoint it with sesame oil, and burn it according to the ritual procedure. Having caused those things of the nature of substances to melt, one should then pour that [liquid] back in its entirety.
Having diligently and with a well-restrained mind produced a form of previous proportions, beautiful, superior to the former, and with a perfectly complete body;
Preceded by the offering of water (argha) according to the ritual procedure for worship.

One should quickly fashion a beautiful form, or a body more complete than before, according to the previous measurements; then, with diligent effort and a courageous nature, one should perform worship preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*argha*).
Having delivered one's own seed-syllable, which is endowed with gnosis and of the nature of the primordial essence, from the belly of Kumbhoda into the image,
by means of the sequence of the offering to be described;
One should perform the consecration quickly according to this very procedure.

Having extracted one's own seed-syllable from the belly of the vase, one should cause the wisdom-family to abide within the physical form. Through that supreme worship which becomes an offering, there is a sequence; swiftly, according to the ritual, it is the consecration.
A stūpa made of baked bricks or stone that is neither decayed nor ruined— that very thing is a completely pure object;
when it contains [the relics], it brings about supreme accomplishment for people.
In the same way, one should sprinkle [the image] made of wood, gold, or other materials.

Having thus completely purified all the actual stūpas that have become of the nature of earth and the nature of vajra, one should make them the core; then, for those beings who effect the supreme siddhi, wood should likewise be cast with gold and other materials.
Indeed, the monasteries, palaces, houses, pavilions, and celestial abodes are manifested as the image of Vairocana;
having extracted them from their formal configuration, they are situated within the space of the bell.
Having established it according to the previous rule, he should perform the ritual.

Having clearly meditated upon the temples, palaces, houses, guest-halls, and shrines as being of the nature of Vairocana, and having properly summoned them from their true abode, one should place them within the vase and perform the ritual correctly according to the previous procedure.
Having performed the auspicious rites of the fire-oblation, the ritual services, and the food-offerings, and having fully satisfied the preeminent sages with abundant gifts,
one should perform the worship for a full hundred years.
When this is done, it will bring benefit to all the world.

Having performed the fire sacrifice, the offerings, the torma, the feast, and the auspicious rites, one should thoroughly please the infinite individuals who are sages; one should fully prepare the ornaments for service and worship. By acting in this way, the benefit of the entire world will be attained.
Thus concludes the procedure for the value of the restoration of a ruined [shrine].
Thus concludes the ritual for the *argha* offering for the restoration of the ancient [deities].
Here, according to the requirements among the procedures to be described,
the vessels for the water for the feet, for sprinkling, for sipping, and for the offering (arghya) may be made of gold, silver, stone, copper, wood, clay, pearl, conch-shell, or a leaf-cup.

In that regard, having placed barley, milk, white flowers, kuśa grass, sesame seeds, parched grain, nectar, and scented water into a single vessel, one should consecrate it seven times or one hundred and eight times with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* and with the mantra of one's own lord for the sake of pacification.

Here, as appropriate in the rituals being explained, [the materials are]: gold, silver, copper, stone, wood, clay, conch, cowrie shells, and mother-of-pearl; vessels for the foot-washing water, the *bsang* offering, the face-cleansing water, and the *argha* (offering water). Within one of those vessels, place barley, milk, and white flowers.

Pour white fragrant water containing *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, parched rice, and nectar; then consecrate it seven times or one hundred and eight times with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, the mantra of one’s own lord, and the *āvartana* mantra, for the purpose of pacification.
For the purpose of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one should cast sesame seeds, curd, yellow flowers, *darpa* grass, nectar, and yellow fragrant water, and likewise recite the mantra.
For the purpose of enrichment (*vṛddhi*), one should pour sesame seeds, curd, yellow flowers, *durba* grass, nectar, and yellow fragrant water, and likewise perform the recitation.

Then, on one's own left side, one should place the vessel for the *argha* offering, the vessel for the *pādya* water, the vessel for the *prokṣaṇa* sprinkling, and the vessel for the *ācamana* rinsing; in front of these, there should also be three separate receiving vessels.

Then, on one's own left side, one should place the *argha* vessel, the *pādya* vessel, the vessel for the *prokṣaṇa* sprinkling, and the vessel for the *ācamana* rinsing. In front of those, there should be three separate receiving vessels.

There, taking water from the vessel for the feet (*pādyabhājana*) with the left fist and a flower with the thumb and index finger joined like a pincer, one should offer it three times into the vessel while gracefully rotating the fingers, using the mantra to be stated hereafter, releasing the fingers in sequence: first the index, then the middle, then the ring, and finally the little finger. One should sprinkle [the vessel] three times with water from the second vessel, held at the tip of the *kuśa*-grass bundle held in the left hand. The same applies when sprinkling the second recipient with water from the all-purpose flask (*sārvakarmikakalaśa*).

Taking water from the second vessel with the left fist and grasping a flower with the thumb and index finger joined as a pincer, one should offer it three times with the fist turned downward while reciting the mantra to be stated below, for the sake of *ācamana* (sipping water), to the second recipient alone; releasing the fingers in sequence—starting with the little finger, then the ring finger, the middle finger, and finally the index finger. Then, taking the water and other substances from the third *argha* vessel with both hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, [one should say]: *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ, accept this supreme and excellent *argha*, hūṃ svāhā*.

Reciting thus, one should offer [the water] by opening the vajra-añjali. Three times; on the third occasion, for the recipient, one should recite the verses for the foot-washing (pādya), sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and sipping (ācamana), omitting the guest-offering (argha) from the previous three rites.

In front of them are also three single-mouthed vessels for receiving [offerings]. Then, from the vessel for the foot-washing water, one takes up water and flowers with the tips of the thumb and index finger of the right hand in the manner of a fist, circling the teeth; then, while reciting the mantra that will be explained, one gradually releases the index, middle, ring, and little fingers in succession.

One should offer [water] into the vessel three times. Having taken water from the second vessel with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass held in the right hand, one should perform the purification (*prokṣaṇa*) three times over the second vessel, the bowl for the mouth; likewise, one should again perform the purification with water from the vase of all activities (*sarvakarmika-kalaśa*).

From the second vessel, holding water and flowers with the thumb and forefinger of the right hand in a fist-like grip, one recites the mantra that will be explained for the second face while offering them as a mouth-rinse.

With the fist turned downward, one should release the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, and index finger in succession and offer [the water] three times. Third, holding the water from the arghya vessel and so forth with cupped hands: oṃ āḥ hrīḥ pravara-satkāra-arghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā.

Reciting thus, one should offer [the substances] three times individually into the three vessels with the vajra-palms opened. For the three previous rites, one should recite *pādyaṃ*, *prokṣaṇaṃ*, and *ācamanaṃ* in place of *arghaṃ*.
This is the procedure characterized by the offering of the *argha* and other [substances].
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the water for offerings and so forth.
